haiku-low.q1: On-call runs the failover command targeting B after probes page them (2 of 3 locations see 3 failed /healthz checks). Detection does nothing automatically; nothing fails over on its own.
haiku-low.q2: Step 3 stops the run, shows the lag, and releases the lock. On-call either reruns with the accept-data-loss override or runs abort. The log keeps its place.
haiku-low.q3: Before promotion: A fenced (active_region=B, best-effort privilege revoke, 20 s wait) and lag checked. Before B's workers start: promotion and requeuing of running jobs. Before DNS: B scaled and passing health checks.
haiku-low.q4: It is lost. B's Redis holds no sessions from A, so every user must sign in again.
haiku-low.q5: It is snapshotted so lost writes can be reviewed, then wiped and rebuilt from a base backup of B as B's replica. No automatic failback.
haiku-low.q6: Self-fencing: every A instance and worker reads active_region every 5 s and writes only after a successful read within 15 s naming its own region. Otherwise it goes read-only, so A stops committing within 20 s.
haiku-low.q7: The control store, a 3-node strongly consistent key-value cluster with nodes in A, B and C. Only the failover command, including abort, writes it. All app instances and workers in both regions read it every 5 s.
haiku-low.q8: Step 5 sets jobs marked running by A's workers back to queued in B's database. B's workers rerun them after step 6. Jobs must be idempotent, keyed by job id, so reruns are safe.
haiku-low.q9: Rerun the command. It takes the lock and resumes at the first step not logged done, repeating any started but unfinished step. Abort is allowed only until step 4 is logged started. After that, no return to A.
haiku-low.q10: Requests still go to A until cached DNS expires, up to 60 s after step 8. If A is up, reads are served from stale data and writes get 503. If A is down, requests fail. After expiry they reach B.
haiku-low.q11: Only commits A made that B never received, since replication is asynchronous. If A failed outright, at most B's recorded lag, held to 30 s unless overridden. If partitioned, A's commits until it stopped writing, up to 20 s after step 2, are also lost.

sonnet.q1: On-call manually runs the failover command (target B). Detection (2 of 3 probe locations seeing 3 consecutive /healthz failures) only pages on-call; nothing fails over automatically.
sonnet.q2: If B's recorded lag (as of last WAL received from A) is over 30 s, the run stops, shows the lag, and releases the lock. On-call then either reruns with the accept-data-loss override (proceeds to promotion) or aborts. Nothing can write meanwhile.
sonnet.q3: Before promoting B's database: the lock is taken, A is fenced (active_region = B, best-effort privilege revoke, 20 s wait), and the lag check passed or was overridden. Before B's workers start: step 5 requeued jobs marked running, after promotion (step 4 done). Before DNS points at B: B passes /healthz at its load balancer and from the probes (step 7), after scale-up.
sonnet.q4: B's Redis holds no sessions from A (not replicated), so every user must sign in again; this is accepted.
sonnet.q5: No automatic failback. A's old database is snapshotted so the lost writes can be reviewed, then wiped and rebuilt from a base backup of B as B's replica. Returning to A is a separate, planned switchover.
sonnet.q6: The self-fencing rule: A's instances/workers write only if a successful control-store read within the last 15 s named A. With active_region = B (or if A can't reach the control store majority), A stops committing within 20 s, and step 2 waits 20 s before proceeding. The privilege revoke is only a best-effort backstop.
sonnet.q7: The control store (3-node strongly consistent KV cluster, nodes in A, B and C) holds active_region. Only the failover command (including abort) writes it; every app instance and worker in both regions reads it every 5 s.
sonnet.q8: Step 5, in B's promoted database before any B worker starts, sets jobs marked running back to queued; B's workers rerun them after step 6. Jobs A finished in its last unreplicated seconds also rerun. Jobs must be idempotent (keyed by job id).
sonnet.q9: Rerun the failover command: it takes the lock (a crashed run's 30 s lease expires within 30 s) and resumes at the first step not logged done; a started-but-unfinished step is repeated (all steps are safe to repeat). Going back to A via failover --abort is possible only until step 4 is logged as started; after that abort is refused, even after a crash mid-promotion, and there is no return to A during this incident.
sonnet.q10: From step 2 until its cached DNS expires (up to 60 s after step 8), its requests still go to A. If A is up, its instances are self-fenced: reads work from A's stale database, writes get 503 'read-only, retry shortly'. If A is down, requests fail. After the TTL expires, the client reaches B.
sonnet.q11: B replays all WAL it received, so the loss is what A committed that B never received (async replication). If A failed outright, at most B's recorded lag, held to 30 s by step 3 unless the override is used. If A kept running after B stopped receiving (partition), A's commits until it stopped writing (at latest 20 s after step 2) are also lost; step 3 can't see these. They survive only in A's old database snapshot.
